elements.content: Communication Goal: I can talk about everyday objects, say what I use, and ask about habits.

Lesson overview:
- Level: A0 General English
- Unit: Unit 3. What is it?
- Time: 60 min (Essential) / 90 min (Expanded) / 120 min (Full Workshop)
- Focus: What do you use every day?
- Materials: Real devices or pictures, survey sheet, COSYmanuals 'present simple' and 'have got' pages.
By the end of this lesson, you can:

• talk about everyday objects
• use present simple negatives
• ask Do/Does questions about habits
Recycling & Course Continuity:

Prior learning: Recycles object vocabulary and present simple.

Next lesson: Lesson 6 recycles everyday objects to talk about hobbies.
Quick retrieval task: which words or phrases do you remember?
Which word belongs to the previous lesson?
Core Active Vocabulary (15 items):

phone — a device for calls and messages. Example: My phone number is 078-452-9103.
computer — a machine for work and the internet. Example: I use my computer every day.
watch — a small clock you wear. Example: My watch is on my wrist.
use — to do something with an object. Example: I use my phone for work.
have — to own or hold something. Example: I have a new bag.
every day — each day. Example: I study English every day.
work — a job or activity you do. Example: I work in an office.
study — to learn about a subject. Example: She studies English at school.
alarm — a sound that wakes you up. Example: My alarm rings at six.
morning — the early part of the day. Example: I check messages in the morning.
need — to require something. Example: I need my phone for work.
often — many times. Example: How often do you use it?
always — every time. Example: I always drink water.
never — not at any time. Example: He never drinks coffee.
don't — the short negative form of do not. Example: I don't use my computer in the morning.
Essential Chunks & Functional Collocations:

• I use my phone every day. (talking about a habit)
• I don't use my computer in the morning. (negative habit)
• Do you use a watch? (yes/no question)
• Does she use a computer for work? (third-person question)
• I need my phone for work. (explaining purpose)
• How often do you use it? (asking about frequency)
Vocabulary practice: choose the correct word.
Which word means 'a device for calls and messages'?
Which word means 'a machine for work and the internet'?
Complete the sentence with a word from the list.
Pronunciation Focus: The /juː/ sound in 'use' and third-person -s

use /juːz/ — voiced /z/ at the end
computer /kəmˈpjuːtə/ — stress the second syllable
watch /wɒtʃ/ — one syllable
alarm /əˈlɑːm/ — stress the second syllable
Listen and repeat:
I use my phone every day. She uses her computer for work.

elements.content: Grammar Focus: Use the present simple for habits, routines, facts, and things that happen regularly.

Form:
Present simple: I / You / We / They + verb. He / She / It + verb + -s. Negative: don't / doesn't + verb. Question: Do / Does + subject + verb?

Examples:
• I work in a school.
• She works in a hospital.
• We don't work on Sunday.
• Does he drink coffee?
Controlled practice: choose the correct form.
He ___ tea every morning.
They ___ in a hospital.
She ___ like coffee.
___ you work here?
Substitution drill: say the sentence with the new words.

• I ... (work / study / live) in ...
• He ... (work / study / live) in ...
• They ... (don't / doesn't) ... on Sunday.
Question-answer practice: ask and answer with your partner.

• What do you do every day?
• Where does your best friend work or study?
• Do you drink coffee in the morning?
Personalised production: use the structure about your own life.

• Write three sentences about your daily routine.
• Write three sentences about a family member's routine.
Reading: What do you use every day?

I have a phone and a computer. I use my phone every day. I don't use my computer in the morning. I use it for work and study in the afternoon. My sister has a watch. She doesn't use her phone at night. Do you use a computer for work? Does your sister use a watch? My alarm rings at seven. I need my phone for work. How often do you use your phone?
When does the writer use the computer?
Does the sister use her phone at night?
Listening: listen to the dialogue and answer the questions.

A: Do you use a computer for work?
B: Yes, I do. I use it every day.
A: Does your sister use a watch?
B: No, she doesn't. She uses her phone.
A: Do you use your phone in the morning?
B: No, I don't. I check messages in the afternoon.
A: How often do you use your computer?
B: I use it five days a week.
Does the speaker use a computer for work?
How often does the speaker use a computer?
Speaking task: Survey your partner about the objects they use. Ask three Do/Does questions and report the answers.

• What do you use every day?
• What don't you use in the morning?
• Do you use a computer for work or study?
• Does your family use watches?
• How often do you use your phone?
Role-play: You are showing a new colleague around the office. Explain what each device is, what you use it for, and what you don't use.
Work in pairs. Take turns. Use at least five target words and one target grammar structure. Then swap roles.
Writing task: Write five sentences about what you use and don't use every day.
Model: I use ... I don't use ... Do you ...? Does she ...?
